## Loading Libraries

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readr)
library(readxl)
library(janitor)
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(plotly)
library(knitr)
library(cowplot)
```

## Reading in Data and Cleaning

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# get economic level data per dissemination area
economic_level_per_da <- read_excel("data/raw/Data sheets & inventory.xlsx", sheet='Overall Analysis') |>
  select(`Economic level (k)...21`:`DA...22`) |>
  drop_na() |>
  rename(economic_level_k = `Economic level (k)...21`,
         dissemination_area = `DA...22`)

plant_shrub_full_data <- read_delim("data/raw/plant_shrub_data.csv", delim=';') |>
  clean_names() |>
  fill(house, .direction = "down")

bird_data <- read_excel("data/raw/BIRDS_spreadsheet2.xlsx", sheet="Long_clean") |>
  clean_names()

# get native percentage
garden_data <- read_excel("data/raw/GARDENS_spreadsheet.xlsx", sheet='Native_vs_not_GRAPHING') |>
  select(House:Economic_level) |> # select necessary columns
  drop_na() |>  # remove empty rows
  clean_names()  # clean column names

native_percent <- garden_data |> # get native percentage per house
  select(house, native_percent_total)

# get main data
stats_data <- read_excel("data/raw/Data sheets & inventory.xlsx", sheet='Everything_statistics') |>
  select(House:Tree_percentage) |>  # select necessary columns
  drop_na() |>  # remove empty rows
  clean_names() |>  # clean column names
  mutate(dissemination_area = as.factor(str_sub(house, 1, 2))) |> # add dissemination area
  left_join(native_percent, by = join_by(house)) # add native percentage
```

## OSFL, BARS, NOFL, PIWO, CBCH, CEDW, VATH, PAWR, RBNU

### Time of day detection

```{r}
bird_subset_data <- bird_data |>
  filter(species %in% c("OSFL", "BARS", "NOFL", "PIWO", "CBCH", "CEDW", "VATH", "PAWR", "RBNU"))

ggplot(bird_subset_data, aes(x = hour)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill="skyblue", colour="white") +
  facet_wrap(~species, scales = "free_y", axes = "all_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 4:12) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Detection Time Distribution by Species",
    x = "Hour of Day",
    y = "Number of Detections"
  )
```

Per House:

```{r, fig.height=10}
ggplot(bird_subset_data, aes(x = hour, y = house, colour = house)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title = "Species of Interest Detection Time Per House",
       x = "Hour of Day",
       y = "House") +
  facet_wrap(~species, scales = "free_y", axes = "all_x")
```

### Economic level

```{r, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
bird_house_data <- bird_subset_data |>
  distinct(house, species)
  
bird_stats_data <- stats_data |>
  filter(house %in% bird_house_data$house) |>
  full_join(bird_house_data, by="house")

ggplot(bird_stats_data, aes(x=economic_level, y= species)) +

```

## Logistic Regression with Mixed Effects for Presence/Absence of a Species

A logistic regression model is well suited to analyze the effect of different variables on a binary outcome (in this case, the presence or absence of a species at a house). Again, we'll be incorporating **mixed effects** into our model due to the sampling scheme. Recall:

> Samples were taken per dissemination area. This means that our data points are **not** independent of each other. Instead, subsets of the data points share a correlation structure. To take this into account, we use **mixed effects** models so observations of the same dissemination area can share the same **random effect/intercept**, making a correlation structure. This is denoted by `(1 | dissemination_area)` in the model code.

However, we might not be able to use this model this for species that are either present at nearly every house or absent from nearly all houses.

Quick look at number of unique houses per species:

```{r}
n_houses_per_species <- bird_data |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(n_houses = n_distinct(house)) |>
  arrange(n_houses)

kable(n_houses_per_species)
```

### Logistic Regression Model: Olive-Sided Flycatcher (OSFL)

In this example, we'll model the presence/absence of the olive-sided flycatcher with economic level (k), number of fruiting species, number of flowering species, and number of grain species at each house. The chosen explanatory variables are chosen just for demonstration purposes, and we'll likely settle on a different set of variables for the final model.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# get data necessary for modeling
plant_shrub_full_data <- read_csv("data/processed/cleaned_plant_shrub_data.csv")

stats_garden_data <- left_join(stats_data, garden_data, by="house", suffix = c("", ".y")) |>
  select(-ends_with(".y"))

osfl_houses <- bird_stats_data |>
  filter(species == "OSFL") |>
  distinct(house)

plant_shrub_data_summarized <- plant_shrub_full_data |>
  group_by(house) |>
  summarize(
    number_fruiting_species = sum(fruiting),
    number_flowering_species = sum(flowering),
    number_grain_species = sum(grain),
  )

stats_garden_data <- left_join(stats_garden_data, plant_shrub_data_summarized, by="house")

osfl_stats_garden_data <- stats_garden_data |>
  mutate(osfl_present = house %in% osfl_houses$house) |>
  mutate(osfl_present = case_when(osfl_present == FALSE ~ 0,
                                  osfl_present == TRUE ~ 1))
```

Ideally, the data would have a good distinction between the outcomes in terms of the predictors for a logistic regression model, such as the following:

![](images/clipboard-1987949782.png)

If we just look at economic level as a singular predictor, we can see that it is difficult to model the distinction between the two outcomes using only economic level. Using more/different predictors would likely help.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(osfl_stats_garden_data) +
  geom_point(aes(economic_level, osfl_present)) +
  geom_smooth(aes(economic_level, osfl_present),
    method = "glm", formula = y ~ x,
    method.args = c(family = binomial), se = FALSE, color = "blue"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 1),
    labels = c("Absent", "Present")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Olive-Sided Flycatcher Presence at Houses vs. Economic Level",
    x = "Economic Level (k)",
    y = "Presence"
  )
```

Let's fit an example logistic regression model with mixed effects, using multiple predictors. Again, this set of predictors is just for demonstration purposes! We'll refine which predictors are used in the model later.

```{r}
osfl_model <- glmer(
  osfl_present ~
    economic_level +
    number_fruiting_species +
    number_flowering_species +
    number_grain_species +
    (1 | dissemination_area),
  data = osfl_stats_garden_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(osfl_model)$coefficients |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(odds_estimate = exp(Estimate),
         odds_estimate_inverted = 1/odds_estimate) |>
  kable()
```

From this, we can see that none of the predictors have a significant effect on the presence of the olive-sided flycatcher at the houses since their p-values (Pr>|z|) > alpha = 0.05.

If they were significant, we'd interpret their effect as the following:

- **Number of fruiting species**: For an increase in one fruiting species in a backyard, it is **1.46 (inverted odds estimate) times** more likely that the bird species will be **absent** instead of present, keeping every other variable constant. OR for an increase in one fruiting species in a backyard, it is **0.68 (odds estimate) times** likely that the bird will be **present** instead of absent, keeping every other variable constant.
- **Number of flowering species**: For an increase in one flowering species in a backyard, it is **1.95 (odds estimate) times** more likely that the bird species will be **present** instead of absent, keeping every other variable constant.
- **Number of grain species**: For an increase in one grain species in a backyard, it is **1.61 (inverted odds estimate) times** more likely that the bird species will be **absent** instead of present, keeping every other variable constant. OR for an increase in one fruiting species in a backyard, it is **0.62 (odds estimate) times** likely that the bird will be **present** instead of absent, keeping every other variable constant.

**These effect estimates will change as we change which predictors are included in the model!!!**

### Logistic Regression Model: Barn Swallow (BARS)

Now, let's model the presence of the barn swallow as another example.

```{r}
bars_houses <- bird_stats_data |>
  filter(species == "BARS") |>
  distinct(house)

bars_stats_garden_data <- stats_garden_data |>
  mutate(bars_present = house %in% bars_houses$house) |>
  mutate(bars_present = case_when(bars_present == FALSE ~ 0,
                                  bars_present == TRUE ~ 1))

bars_model <- glmer(
  bars_present ~
    economic_level +
    number_fruiting_species +
    number_flowering_species +
    number_grain_species +
    (1 | dissemination_area),
  data = bars_stats_garden_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(bars_model)$coefficients |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(odds_estimate = exp(Estimate),
         odds_estimate_inverted = 1/odds_estimate) |>
  kable()
```

From this, we can again see that none of the predictors have a significant effect on the presence of the barn swallow at the houses since their p-values (Pr>|z|) > alpha = 0.05.

If they were significant, we'd interpret the effect of following as:

- **Number of flowering species**: For an increase in one flowering species in a backyard, it is **1.27 (inverted odds estimate) times** more likely that the bird species will be **absent** instead of present, keeping every other variable constant. OR for an increase in one fruiting species in a backyard, it is **0.79 (odds estimate) times** likely that the bird will be **present** instead of absent, keeping every other variable constant.
- **Number of grain species**: For an increase in one grain species in a backyard, it is **5.77 (inverted odds estimate) times** more likely that the bird species will be **absent** instead of present, keeping every other variable constant. OR for an increase in one fruiting species in a backyard, it is **0.17 (odds estimate) times** likely that the bird will be **present** instead of absent, keeping every other variable constant.

**These effect estimates will change as we change which predictors are included in the model!!!**
